results.title: Do Grounding Sheets Work? - Amerisleep
results.content: * Grounding sheets lack substantial scientific evidence to support their claimed benefits. * Evidence-based approaches to improving sleep quality are more reliable than grounding sheets. Your money would be better spent on proven sleep products like a quality mattress, comfortable bedding made from natural fibers, blackout curtains, or a white noise machine. You’ve probably seen ads for special bed sheets that plug into your wall outlet, promising better sleep and improved health through “earthing” or “grounding.”. These sheets claim to connect you with the Earth’s natural electrical field while you sleep, supposedly helping your body release harmful electrical charges and absorb beneficial electrons. Read on to learn the truth about grounding sheets and discover what really works for better sleep. Grounding sheets are specialized bedding products that contain conductive materials and connect to your electrical outlet’s grounding port. Sleep medicine specialists and mainstream scientists remain highly skeptical about grounding sheets and their supposed benefits. There’s no concrete evidence showing a connection between grounding devices and measurable improvements in sleep quality or health outcomes. When reputable sleep organizations publish guidelines for better sleep, grounding products never make the list of evidence-based recommendations. If you’re considering grounding sheets because you struggle with serious sleep problems, schedule an appointment with your doctor instead. Many people make other positive lifestyle changes at the same time they try grounding sheets, like going to bed earlier or reducing screen time, which actually cause the improvements. While some grounding sheet manufacturers claim their products reduce inflammation and chronic pain, scientific evidence supporting these claims remains limited and inconclusive. While grounding sheets won’t harm children, focusing on consistent bedtimes, limited screen time before bed, and comfortable bedding will likely have a much greater impact on your child’s sleep quality. Grounding sheets make big promises about improving your sleep, but the scientific evidence and testing results suggest you should approach these claims with healthy skepticism. You can certainly try grounding sheets if you’re curious, but set realistic expectations and don’t count on dramatic improvements in your sleep quality or health. Before investing in specialized grounding sheets, consider trying proven sleep strategies like consistent bedtimes, creating a comfortable sleep environment, and limiting screen time before bed.

results.content:
Title: Watch: Controversial bat-pad call rules Kohli out for a duck after third umpire finds evidence inconclusive
# Watch: Controversial bat-pad call rules Kohli out for a duck after third umpire finds evidence inconclusive. Watch: Virat Kohli’s return to the India side was marred by controversy as he was given lbw with a tight bat-pad decision going against him in the second Test against New Zealand. Virender Sharma, the TV umpire asked for UltraEdge, which showed a spike when the ball was close to the bat. Further replays suggesting that the ball might have touched the bat and the pad simultaneously. I don’t have any conclusive evidence to overturn that,” stated Sharma, who asked Chaudhary to give Kohli out without looking at the ball tracking. Sharma asked for the ball tracking upon being reminded by Chaudhary, which showed three reds as Kohli walked back in disbelief. Clause 36.2.2 of the MCC Laws of Cricket states that “if the ball makes contact with the striker’s person and bat simultaneously, this shall be considered as the ball having first touched the bat.”. The Laws of Cricket occasionally differ from the ICC playing conditions in subtle ways, and the same clause in the ICC’s rule book states, “if the bowler’s end umpire is not satisfied that the ball intercepted the batsman’s person before it touched the bat, the batsman shall be given not out.”. Sanjay Bangar, former India batting coach, disagreed with the decision, suggesting that there was a clear deviation before the ball hit the pad. Speaking on *Star Sports* during the lunch break, Bangar said, “I certainly felt the ball hit the bat first. Clearly, the ball hit the bat first. Now, for the ball to come back and hit the pad, it is only because there is something on it. “Everyone in the commentary box thought it hit the pad first and then went back on the bat and then on the pad. The images clearly show the ball clipping on the pad first, then going on to the bat then the pad again. If you see the line of the ball, it can’t hit the bat first because the bat is behind the pad anyway.

results.content:
Title: Reducing Inconclusive Results: A Descriptive Analysis of Decision Rules, Weighted Electrodermal Scores and Multinomial Cut-Scores | Polygraph Research | LieDetectorTest.com – Lie Detector Test
Reducing Inconclusive Results: A Descriptive Analysis of Decision Rules, Weighted Electrodermal Scores and Multinomial Cut-Scores. # Reducing Inconclusive Results: A Descriptive Analysis of Decision Rules, Weighted Electrodermal Scores and Multinomial Cut-Scores. Weighted EDA scores alone reduced inconclusive results by 49%, while combining EDA weighting with multinomial cut-scores achieved a 72% reduction in inconclusive outcomes. This study examined how different scoring methodologies affect inconclusive polygraph results by analyzing weighted electrodermal scores and multinomial cut-scores using archival field data. The research found that combining weighted EDA scores with multinomial cut-scores reduced inconclusive results by an average of 72%. The study used descriptive statistics and point estimates to analyze archival field polygraph data from confirmed single-issue investigations, comparing different decision rules, EDA weighting approaches, and traditional versus multinomial cut-scores. This research addressed the persistent problem of inconclusive polygraph results by systematically analyzing scoring methodologies using archival field data from confirmed single-issue investigations. The study compared traditional unweighted scoring with weighted electrodermal activity scores and examined the impact of multinomial cut-scores derived from Bayesian statistical frameworks. Results showed that EDA weighting alone reduced inconclusive rates by 49%, while the combination of weighted EDA scores and multinomial cut-scores achieved a 72% reduction. This study explores whether strategically weighting EDA scores and applying statistically-derived decision thresholds could substantially reduce inconclusive outcomes without sacrificing accuracy. The researchers used descriptive statistics and point estimates to study the effect on inconclusive results and other metrics of test accuracy, analyzing data as a function of different decision rules, structural weighting of sensor scores, and cut-scores. **Weighted EDA scores produced an average 49% reduction of inconclusive results across all decision rules, and the combination of weighted EDA scores and multinomial cut-scores reduced the occurrence of inconclusive results by an average of 72%**. Use of different decision rules had less effect with the multinomial cut-scores, suggesting that the statistical optimization provided by the multinomial approach reduces sensitivity to procedural variations in how scores are combined. Examiners who score charts manually may experience different benefits from EDA weighting and multinomial cut-scores. For polygraph examiners, this research provides strong empirical support for adopting EDA-weighted scoring systems and multinomial cut-scores.

results.content:
Title: Rollback deployment on metric threshold - Render
# Rollback deployment on metric threshold. I want to be able to automatically trigger a deployment rollback if the deployment succeeds, but within a certain timeframe, some metric thresholds are triggered (memory %, CPU, bandwidth, etc). This feels like quite a narrow and potentially complex use case. One case that springs to mind, is if the service had autoscaling enabled, increased resource use would scale more instances rather than rollback. In addition, a rollback wouldn’t revert any database migrations made in the latest deploy, so automatically rolling back could potentially leave the service in a broken state if migrations are part of your deploy process and don’t line up with the previous deploys code. I’ve tried to think if there’s a way to recreate that behavior with the current feature set, but I don’t think there is, as rollbacks are not yet part of the API. However, please feel free to add this as a feature request to our feedback site, so that it can be reviewed by our team and other customers.
